body:
What changed in the method of struggle?

The Civil Disobedience Movement continued the Gandhian methods of non-violence, boycott and public mobilisation, but it placed greater emphasis on the deliberate violation of specific colonial laws. This is the central distinction between the Non-Cooperation Movement and the Civil Disobedience Movement.

Non-Cooperation chiefly aimed to weaken colonial rule by refusing to assist British-controlled institutions. Civil disobedience went further: people openly challenged laws and government demands that they considered unjust.

FeatureNon-Cooperation MovementCivil Disobedience Movement
Main period1920–19221930–1934
Principal methodWithdrawal of cooperation from colonial institutionsOpen defiance of selected colonial laws, alongside boycotts
Typical actionsBoycott of government schools, courts, councils and foreign goodsBreaking salt and forest laws, refusing specified taxes, and boycotting foreign goods
Gandhian principleNon-violent resistanceNon-violent resistance
Major ending or interruptionWithdrawn in February 1922Suspended in March 1931, revived in 1932 and ended in 1934

The methods overlapped. Boycotts occurred in both movements, and resistance to taxes had appeared in earlier struggles. The distinction concerns the central programme and emphasis, not an absolute separation of activities.

Forms of protest during the 1930 campaign

Breaking the salt law

People collected or manufactured salt without obeying colonial restrictions. Coastal salt-making was particularly suitable because seawater and natural salt were available. Protesters also demonstrated near government salt establishments.

Refusal to pay taxes and revenue

In several areas, peasants refused to pay land revenue demanded by the government. In parts of eastern India, villagers refused to pay the chaukidari tax, a local tax associated with village watchmen who performed policing duties.

These actions targeted colonial revenue collection. They were more than expressions of disagreement: non-payment was a refusal to comply with a legal financial demand.

Violation of forest laws

Some communities entered reserved forests to graze cattle or collect wood in violation of colonial regulations. Forest restrictions affected the everyday livelihoods of people who depended on forests. Consequently, breaking a forest law could connect the national campaign to a direct local grievance.

Boycott and picketing

Foreign cloth was boycotted, and protesters demonstrated outside shops selling foreign cloth or liquor. Picketing means organising a protest at or near an establishment to discourage people from entering or purchasing goods there.

Not every boycott or peaceful picket was itself an illegal act. Such methods remained part of the wider campaign even though deliberate law-breaking was its defining feature.

Withdrawal from government service

Village officials were encouraged to resign rather than assist colonial administration. This resembled the earlier strategy of non-cooperation and complemented the new programme of law-breaking.

The difference between land revenue and rent

Land revenue was a government demand on land or agricultural production. Rent was generally paid by a tenant to the landlord from whom land was rented. Therefore, refusing government revenue and refusing rent owed to a landlord affected different parties.

This distinction became important because poorer tenants sometimes wanted unpaid rent cancelled, whereas many better-off cultivators chiefly sought reductions in government revenue.

Non-violence was the intended method, not a description of every incident. Gandhi instructed satyagrahis to avoid violence, but clashes and violent outbreaks occurred in some places as the movement spread and the authorities attempted to suppress it.

Prelims focus

  • Civil disobedience: Deliberate violation of unjust laws.
  • Non-cooperation: Withdrawal of support from colonial institutions.
  • Salt law: Broken by collecting or making salt outside permitted government arrangements.
  • Forest laws: Defied through prohibited grazing and collection of forest products.
  • Chaukidari tax: Associated with village watchmen.
  • Trap: Land revenue paid to government and rent paid to a landlord were not the same obligation.

[NCERT, India and the Contemporary World–II, Class 10, 'Nationalism in India', printed pp. 56–58 and 63–65; NCERT, Our Pasts–III, Class 8, 'The Making of the National Movement: 1870s–1947', printed pp. 117–122; IGNOU, Indian National Movement, Unit 15, sections 15.3–15.4, 'The Lahore Session' and 'Spread of the Movement'.]

pictures.alt: Civil Disobedience branches into direct law-breaking, refusal of legal dues and continuing non-cooperation, all guided by non-violent action.
pictures.caption: Civil disobedience combined direct law-breaking with revenue resistance and continuing boycotts.

title: Methods of Civil Disobedience and Their Difference from Non-Cooperation

body:
The campaign spreads beyond Dandi

Gandhi's violation of the salt law on 6 April 1930 encouraged similar actions elsewhere. The Civil Disobedience Movement was not confined to the Gujarat coast. In different provinces, local leaders adapted the programme to the conditions and grievances of their communities.

Important regional centres

  • Tamil Nadu: C. Rajagopalachari, also known as Rajaji, led the Vedaranyam Salt Satyagraha. His march began at Tiruchirapalli on 13 April 1930 and proceeded towards the coast at Vedaranyam.
  • Malabar: K. Kelappan led a salt satyagraha march from Calicut, now Kozhikode, towards Payyanur.
  • Odisha: Gopabandhu Choudhury led satyagrahis towards the coastal salt-making centre of Inchudi.
  • North-West Frontier Province: Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan and his followers, associated with the non-violent Khudai Khidmatgar movement, participated in the wider anti-colonial agitation. Peshawar witnessed major demonstrations in April 1930.
  • Bihar and Bengal: Campaigns against the chaukidari tax became important forms of civil disobedience where the salt issue was less directly suited to local conditions.

These examples show how one national programme could take different forms. Coastal areas could organise salt-making, while inland districts might focus on taxes, forest restrictions or other colonial institutions.

The government's response

The British administration responded with arrests, prohibitory orders, attacks on demonstrations and other coercive measures. Nationalist leaders were detained, and peaceful protesters were sometimes beaten. The repression did not always stop public agitation; in some places, an arrest triggered fresh demonstrations.

In April 1930, the arrest of Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan was followed by major unrest in Peshawar. After Gandhi's arrest in May, industrial workers and others demonstrated in Sholapur, where attacks on institutions associated with British rule occurred.

As repression intensified, roughly 100,000 people were arrested during the 1930 phase, according to a commonly cited textbook estimate. This is an approximate figure, not a precise count of every detention throughout 1930–1934.

Gandhi's arrest at Karadi

After the Dandi action, Gandhi continued organising resistance and planned further action against the government salt works at Dharasana in Gujarat.

Before he could lead that campaign, Gandhi was arrested at Karadi on 5 May 1930. His arrest did not end the salt satyagraha. Other leaders continued the planned protests.

The Dharasana Salt Satyagraha

Abbas Tyabji led a group of satyagrahis towards Dharasana on 12 May 1930, but he and other marchers were arrested. Sarojini Naidu subsequently took a leading role in the campaign.

On 21 May 1930, groups of unarmed satyagrahis attempted to approach the Dharasana salt works. Police attacked protesters with lathis. The severe beating of non-violent volunteers was reported by journalists and attracted international attention. Sarojini Naidu was arrested during the action.

Dharasana and Dandi were separate places and separate stages of the Salt Satyagraha. The Dandi action began the public violation of the salt law on 6 April; the Dharasana campaign continued the struggle after Gandhi's arrest.

Why the repression mattered

Police action revealed the conflict between a government determined to enforce its laws and protesters who deliberately refused obedience. The Dharasana events were especially significant because the contrast between unarmed satyagrahis and police violence could be understood by audiences outside India as well as within it.

However, the movement was not uniformly peaceful everywhere. Some confrontations developed into violence, especially after arrests or police action. This difference between Gandhi's intended method and the behaviour of every crowd must be kept clear.

Prelims focus

  • C. Rajagopalachari: Vedaranyam Salt Satyagraha in Tamil Nadu.
  • K. Kelappan: Malabar salt march towards Payyanur.
  • Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan: Associated with the Khudai Khidmatgar movement in the North-West Frontier Province.
  • 5 May 1930: Gandhi arrested at Karadi, Gujarat.
  • 21 May 1930: Major Dharasana salt-works protest associated with Sarojini Naidu.
  • Trap: Gandhi broke the salt law at Dandi, but he did not lead the 21 May Dharasana action because he was already under arrest.

[NCERT, India and the Contemporary World–II, Class 10, 'Nationalism in India', printed pp. 64–65; IGNOU, Indian National Movement, Unit 15, section 15.4, 'Spread of the Movement: Popular Response and Regional Pattern'; Government of India, Press Information Bureau, 'Unsung Heroes of Freedom Struggle Remembered in Webinar on Azadi Ka Amrit Mahotsav', 19 August 2021, Vedaranyam section; Gandhi Heritage Portal, 'Events Post March', entries for April–June 1930, accessed 21 November 2026; United Press, Webb Miller's report on the Dharasana salt-works action, 21 May 1930.]

pictures.alt: Timeline of the April 1930 salt protests, Gandhi’s arrest on 5 May, and continued resistance at Dharasana under Tyabji and Naidu.
pictures.caption: Key events in the expansion and repression of the 1930 Salt Satyagraha.

title: The Nationwide Movement, Dharasana Satyagraha and British Repression

body:
Different groups understood swaraj differently

The Civil Disobedience Movement attracted support from several sections of Indian society, but they did not all participate for the same reasons. The Congress presented independence as a common objective, while individual groups often connected that objective to their own economic and social grievances.

This distinction explains both the broad appeal of the movement and the difficulties in maintaining unity when the Congress leadership negotiated with the government.

Rich peasants and the Gujarat connection

Among the active agricultural supporters were the Patidars of Gujarat and the Jats of Uttar Pradesh. Many were relatively prosperous cultivators who produced commercial crops for sale.

When agricultural prices fell during the economic depression, their cash incomes declined. However, government demands for land revenue did not fall accordingly. They therefore supported campaigns seeking relief from revenue payments.

Some rich peasants were disappointed when the movement was suspended in 1931 without a general reduction in land revenue rates. Consequently, many were reluctant to participate in the renewed campaign of 1932.

Poor peasants and tenants

Poorer peasants, especially those who rented land, faced an additional difficulty. Besides agricultural expenses, they owed rent to landlords. When their incomes fell, they wanted relief from unpaid rent.

The Congress was generally reluctant to support broad no-rent campaigns because such demands could alienate landlords and better-off cultivators who also supported the national movement. This created tension between some poorer peasants and the Congress leadership.

Business groups, industrial workers and women

Indian merchants and industrialists opposed colonial economic arrangements that restricted opportunities for Indian enterprise or favoured imports. Business leaders such as G. D. Birla and Purshottamdas Thakurdas supported the movement in its initial phase. The Federation of Indian Chambers of Commerce and Industry (FICCI), established in 1927, was an important organisation representing business interests.

Some business groups supplied financial support and participated in boycotts of imported goods. Their enthusiasm later became less uniform because prolonged agitation, possible violence and conflict between labour and business interests created concerns.

Industrial workers participated in protests and strikes, but their involvement in the Civil Disobedience Movement was generally less extensive than that of peasants in many regions. The Nagpur region was a notable exception. Some workers connected the national struggle to demands concerning wages and working conditions.

Women participated on a large scale. They joined processions, manufactured salt, picketed liquor and foreign-cloth shops, and accepted imprisonment. This expanded women's public political activity, although it did not immediately give women equal authority within Congress organisations.

Participation was not uniform across communities

Some Dalit organisations and leaders, including B. R. Ambedkar, placed particular emphasis on ending caste discrimination and obtaining political representation. Participation in Congress-led civil disobedience was limited in some areas because the Congress programme did not fully address these priorities.

Sections of Muslim political opinion also remained distant from the Congress because of growing communal distrust and disagreements over political representation. However, Muslim participation was not absent. The non-violent movement associated with Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan in the North-West Frontier Province was an important example of active resistance to British rule.

Comparison of major participating groups

GroupImportant concernPattern of participation
Rich peasantsHigh government land revenue despite falling crop pricesRevenue resistance; support weakened after the 1931 suspension
Poor tenantsRent owed to landlordsSome supported more radical no-rent demands
Business groupsTrade restrictions and foreign competitionInitial financial support and boycott of imports
Industrial workersWages and working conditionsSelective participation; important regional exceptions
WomenNational freedom and greater public involvementSalt-making, marches, picketing and imprisonment
Dalit organisationsSocial equality and political safeguardsUneven involvement in Congress-led campaigns
Muslim communitiesNational freedom alongside concerns about political representationVaried involvement, including major mobilisation in the North-West Frontier Province

Participation does not imply identical demands. The movement united people against colonial rule, but rich peasants, poor tenants, business owners, workers and marginalised communities often expected different changes from swaraj.

Prelims focus

  • Patidars of Gujarat and Jats of Uttar Pradesh: Important rich-peasant supporters.
  • Rich peasants: Sought relief from government land revenue.
  • Poor tenants: Often sought relief from rent owed to landlords.
  • G. D. Birla and Purshottamdas Thakurdas: Important business figures associated with nationalist economic demands.
  • Women: Participated in salt-making, picketing and protest marches.
  • Trap: Limited participation by some Muslim or Dalit groups does not mean that every member of those communities stayed outside the movement.

[NCERT, India and the Contemporary World–II, Class 10, 'Nationalism in India', printed pp. 65–69, sections 'How Participants Saw the Movement' and 'The Limits of Civil Disobedience'; NCERT, Our Pasts–III, Class 8, 'The Making of the National Movement: 1870s–1947', printed pp. 121–122; IGNOU, Indian National Movement, Unit 15, section 15.5, 'Social Base of the Movement'.]

pictures.caption: Women participated in public protests, including picketing shops selling foreign cloth and liquor.

title: Participation of Peasants, Women, Business Groups and Other Communities
